documentary.heading: The Pact
documentary.why: The public promise of peace conceals a plan to divide territory. Poland's future is being negotiated without Poland.
documentary.imageNote: A photograph can show the public meeting, but not the secret protocol. Read the diplomatic history alongside the image.
documentary.historySourceLabel: US Holocaust Memorial Museum · invasion and the pact
documentary.narration: Late on 23 August, in the Kremlin, Joachim von Ribbentrop and Vyacheslav Molotov put their names to a ten-year non-aggression treaty between Germany and the Soviet Union. Stalin stays for the toasts. The published text speaks of peace. A secret protocol, which Moscow will deny for fifty years, draws a line through Poland along the Narew, the Vistula and the San, and places Finland, Estonia, Latvia and Bessarabia in the Soviet sphere. Hitler no longer fears a war on two fronts.
documentary.caption: Stalin talks with German Foreign Minister Joachim von Ribbentrop (right) in the Kremlin after the signing of the German-Soviet Non-Aggression Pact, Moscow, 23 August 1939.

documentary.heading: The posters go up
documentary.why: Mobilisation means turning civilians into an organised army. Orders, transport and time matter as much as the number of men on paper.
documentary.imageNote: The catalogue dates this photograph to 30 August. Its later publication in a 1967 book is not the date of the scene.
documentary.historySourceLabel: The National WWII Museum · Poland's preparations
documentary.narration: Poland decides on general mobilisation on 29 August, then holds it back when the British and French ambassadors urge Warsaw not to provoke Hitler. On the afternoon of the 30th the notices are pasted up at last, with the first day of mobilisation set for the 31st. Reservists head for their depots; families crowd the station platforms to see them off. Two days is not enough. Many units will still be on the trains when the war begins.
documentary.caption: A man reads the notice of general mobilisation, posted on 30 August 1939.

documentary.heading: Gleiwitz
documentary.why: This is a manufactured pretext, not a Polish attack. The invasion is already planned; the staged incident supplies a propaganda justification.
documentary.imageNote: This shows the surviving transmitter site, not the attack. No claim is made that the photographer witnessed the events of 1939.
documentary.historySourceLabel: The National WWII Museum · the staged pretext
documentary.narration: On the evening of 31 August a squad of SS men led by Alfred Naujocks seizes the German radio station at Gleiwitz, close to the Polish border, and shouts a few sentences in Polish into a microphone. They leave a body behind: Franciszek Honiok, a 43-year-old Silesian farmer known for his Polish sympathies, arrested the day before, drugged and shot. It is one of several attacks staged that night. By morning Berlin has its 'Polish aggression'.
documentary.caption: The wooden transmitter tower of the former Gleiwitz radio station, scene of the staged attack of 31 August 1939, in today's Gliwice, Poland (modern photograph).

documentary.heading: 04:45, Westerplatte
documentary.why: The attack is not confined to one harbour. Air raids and land offensives strike elsewhere as the invasion begins.
documentary.imageNote: The archive identifies the ship during the bombardment. A still photograph cannot establish the exact minute of the opening salvo.
documentary.historySourceLabel: The National WWII Museum · the invasion
documentary.narration: The old battleship Schleswig-Holstein has lain in Danzig harbour since 25 August on a courtesy visit. In the grey before dawn she opens fire at close range on Westerplatte, the Polish depot across the channel: at 04:45 by the usual reckoning, two or three minutes later by some accounts. Some two hundred defenders under Major Henryk Sucharski will hold out for seven days. Inland, Stukas are already over the little town of Wieluń, and its hospital is hit.
documentary.caption: The German battleship Schleswig-Holstein in the Danzig harbour channel during the bombardment of the Polish garrison at Westerplatte, September 1939.
documentary.credit: Unknown photographer / Instytut Pamięci Narodowej (Institute of National Remembrance)

documentary.heading: Dawn in the Tuchola Forest
documentary.why: The scale now narrows from countries to people. This is the real setting for the fictional journey you are about to play.
documentary.imageNote: The archive identifies Polish prisoners in the Tuchola Forest on 1 September. None of these men is identified as the fictional Wrona.
documentary.historySourceLabel: US Holocaust Memorial Museum · the campaign
documentary.narration: At the same hour, General Heinz Guderian's XIX Corps crosses into the Polish Corridor, the strip of Pomerania that joins Poland to the sea. Ground mist lies so thick among the pines of the Tuchola Forest that German guns fire blind into it, against orders. Ahead of the panzers wait the infantry of Operational Group Czersk and the Pomorska Cavalry Brigade, the 18th Pomeranian Uhlans among them. Before the day is out, the Wehrmacht has taken its first prisoners in the forest.
documentary.caption: Some of the first Polish soldiers taken prisoner by the Wehrmacht, in the Tuchola Forest (Tucheler Heide), 1 September 1939.

briefing.text: Wrona. Sit, if you can find something that isn't moving. The Germans crossed at a quarter to five, all along the line. You know as much as I do, and I know very little. An hour ago a staff car left the Chojnice road in the fog, somewhere in the forest east of here. It was carrying a courier from Warsaw. We heard the shots; we have not heard from the courier. He had a leather dispatch satchel chained to his wrist, sealed for Army Pomorze. Do not ask me what is in it. I was not told, which tells me enough. First, find the car. Second, take the satchel, and do not open it, whatever state it or he is in. Third, bring it back to us through whatever the Germans have put between you and our lines. We fall back on the Brda by nightfall. You go alone and on foot. A horse makes noise, and a squadron makes a battle. Go with God, Lieutenant, and go quietly.

dialogue.line: Fog. The Germans have brought their own weather.
Engines to the west. Many of them. Polite of them to announce themselves.
One man, one knife, one satchel to find. I have been given worse odds by my mother at cards.
Quietly, then. As the Rotmistrz says.

victory.line: The satchel is dry and the seal unbroken: General Staff, Cipher Bureau. Its courier will not need it now. I will see that somebody does.

aftermath.narration: That evening, near Krojanty, two squadrons of the 18th Pomeranian Uhlans charge German infantry in a forest clearing to cover the retreat from Chojnice, and scatter them, until armoured cars appear on the road and open fire. Colonel Kazimierz Mastalerz falls with some twenty of his men. The next day journalists are shown dead horses beside tanks that arrived after the fight, and a myth is born: Polish lancers charging panzers. It never happened. On 3 September Britain and France declare war. By the 5th the Polish divisions in the Tuchola Forest have been broken.
aftermath.caption: Memorial near Krojanty to the soldiers of the 18th Pomeranian Uhlans killed in the charge of 1 September 1939 (photographed 2009).

letter.text:
Mama,
You stood on the platform at Bydgoszcz until the train was out of sight. I watched your hat to the last. Your rosary is in my breast pocket, and today it earned its keep. I am writing by the light of something burning, so forgive the hand. I walked a long way through the pines this morning, alone, and was not afraid until afterwards, which is the correct order. Tell Zosia I have not forgotten her. Do not stand near windows. Do not believe the radio when it sounds cheerful. I promised you I would come home. I keep my word, Mama, even when I am slow about it.
Your son,
Tomasz

facts: The secret protocol of the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact divided Poland along the Narew, Vistula and San rivers. The Soviet Union denied that it existed until 1989.
Franciszek Honiok, killed by the SS and left at the Gleiwitz radio station as 'evidence' of a Polish attack, is often called the first victim of the Second World War.
Schleswig-Holstein's first salvo at Westerplatte is usually timed at 04:45; some historians argue for 04:47 or 04:48. The garrison held out until 7 September.
At Krojanty the 18th Pomeranian Uhlans charged German infantry, not tanks. The story of lances against panzers began with journalists taken to the battlefield the next day.
Poland went to war in 1939 with eleven cavalry brigades. They usually fought dismounted, as mobile infantry with anti-tank rifles and light artillery.

learning.question: How does a country go from diplomacy to invasion in nine days?
learning.connection: The historical offensive is larger than anything one officer can stop. This fictional mission puts you inside a smaller problem: move through the advance, recover a dispatch and get back to your own lines.
learning.boundary: Wrona, Zaremba and the satchel operation are invented. The battlefield is a designed tactical map, not a surveyed reconstruction. Your success does not change the historical outcome.

takeaways.heading: A pact is not the same as peace
takeaways.text: The German–Soviet agreement included a secret division of territory. The Soviet Union invaded eastern Poland on 17 September 1939.

takeaways.heading: Look past the cavalry myth
takeaways.text: Polish cavalry carried rifles, machine guns and anti-tank weapons. The familiar image of lances deliberately attacking tanks misrepresents their war.

takeaways.heading: This morning is only the beginning
takeaways.text: Britain and France declared war on Germany on 3 September. Polish resistance continued into October; defeat brought occupation, not peace.
